title: i left Grok Bot with one side project at 80%, six specialist bots, and...
headline: i left Grok Bot with one side project at 80%, six specialist bots, and one rule: nothing irreversible happens while i sleep the remaining 20% was a chain of small jobs i kept postponing.
body:
i left Grok Bot with one side project at 80%, six specialist bots, and one rule: nothing irreversible happens while i sleep

the remaining 20% was a chain of small jobs i kept postponing. trace the issue back to its source. choose one owner. build on a branch. run the tests. review the change from a clean context. prepare a preview. remember why the decision was made

so i set it up like a tiny night shift

Scout watched the issues and kept every task tied to its source. Chief picked the next owner. Forge built and tested. Critic reviewed work it had not written. Ship prepared the preview. Ledger saved the reasoning for the next run

all six used the same computer, repo, files, browser sessions, and logins. the task moved forward without me copying context from one tool into another

then i removed five inboxes

only Chief was allowed to interrupt me. the other bots handed the work forward quietly, with the source, branch, test output, review, and decision history still attached

when i came back, Chief had reduced the night to one packet: a branch, test output, review notes, a preview, and one decision waiting

merge to main, production deploys, external messages, secrets, spending, and deletion still stopped at the human gate

that is the version of multi-agent work that helped me. six workers moved the project forward while the management came back as one decision

i put the exact charters, schedules, handoff prompt, and rollout order in the article below. look for the sentence repeated in every charter. that sentence is what lets the whole thing run overnight.

Filter kills noise.
Research adds sources.
Writer turns it into angles.

The operator skill is not prompting.

It is designing a system where bad signals die before they reach you.

title: I gave a Grok Bot my logins and let it work
headline: I gave a Grok Bot my logins and let it work.
body:
I gave a Grok Bot my logins and let it work.

Here is what actually happened (and what I would change):

- It runs from its own cloud machine, not my laptop
- It signs into tools as itself, with its own accounts
- I brief it once, then message it like a colleague
- It works the job end to end while I do other things
- It stops and asks before anything irreversible
- Nothing on my drive ever entered the picture

The mental shift took me longer than the setup. I kept writing prompts. It does not want prompts, it wants a standing brief and a role.

Once that landed, the thing I liked most was boring. It came back and asked. Twice on a job I expected it to plough straight through.

What I would change: the tier ladder. Access depends on which Grok or Cursor plan you hold, and until recently that meant the very top ones. That has widened to SuperGrok Plus, Cursor Pro+ and all Cursor Teams plans, plus a 7 day capped trial with a card required.

It is still a beta. Treat it like one, hand it reversible work first, and see how it goes.

headline: I'M A F*CKING GENIUS - I MADE GROK BOT MY CHIEF OF STAFF BEFORE ANYONE ELSE FIGURED OUT IT COULD BE ONE.
body:
I'M A F*CKING GENIUS - I MADE GROK BOT MY CHIEF OF STAFF BEFORE ANYONE ELSE FIGURED OUT IT COULD BE ONE.

And now? Every AI thread on X is preaching it.

Scroll your feed. You've seen it. The pixel-art dashboards. The "8-bot digital office" carousels. The threads breaking down "agent org charts" like they just discovered management theory. Every single one of them is running the setup I posted three weeks ago - and half of them can't even name what the bots are supposed to do.

I DIDN'T HIRE A COFOUNDER. I APPOINTED A CHIEF OF STAFF.

Just look at what my desk looks like now.

Before, AI was a chat window. I typed, it answered, I copied, I moved on. A very expensive typewriter with a good memory.

Now Grok Bot sits at the top of the org chart. It receives my objectives, splits the work across six specialists, catches everything downstream, and only pings me for the four decisions that actually need a human. Send. Spend. Publish. Delete. Everything else runs while I sleep.

And here's the part that made people stop scrolling: it took me one evening to set up.

Download the app → sign in → create the "Chief" role → give the other bots job titles like you would brief new hires → connect Telegram → drop the first goal in the chat.

→ No experience needed.
→ No VPS.
→ No coding.
→ Nothing complicated. At all.

I hand it a target. The Chief breaks it into steps, delegates to the specialists, chases the handoffs, and pushes the finished work back to me for a single yes. That is the whole job now. Yes or no. Four times a day.

Grok Bot is not a chatbot. It is middle management with a shorter attention span and no ego. You can staff a whole desk in one evening, even if you have never touched an agent in your life.

So yeah. The pattern is everywhere.

The credit for figuring it out first? Still with me.

Copy the org chart again. I'll design the next one before you finish reading.

title: 2 rules I use to make sure every Grok Bot agent has one job: 1
headline: 2 rules I use to make sure every Grok Bot agent has one job: 1.
body:
2 rules I use to make sure every Grok Bot agent has one job:

1. Describe the job in one sentence — with no “and.”

Not: “Write the draft and post it.”

Just: “Write the draft.”

2. If there’s another step, give it to another agent.

One researches.
One writes.
One publishes.

One job. One agent.

It sounds simple, but it makes managing an entire agent team much easier.

title: i gave Elon's Grok Bot $50 and told it "pay for yourself or you die"...
headline: i gave Elon's Grok Bot $50 and told it "pay for yourself or you die" 48 hours later it's holding $5,273 and it's still alive autonomous trading agent on polymarket zero code this time.
body:
i gave Elon's Grok Bot $50 and told it "pay for yourself or you die"

48 hours later it's holding $5,273

and it's still alive

autonomous trading agent on polymarket

zero code this time. the bot has its own computer in the cloud, its own browser, its own terminal. it trades with my laptop shut

every 10 minutes it:

→ scans 500-1000 markets
→ reads live X sentiment (it's grok, it sees every post on this app)
→ builds fair value, flags mispricing > 8%
→ calculates position size (kelly criterion, max 6% bankroll)
→ executes in its own browser
→ pays its own $200 subscription from profits

if the balance hits $0, i cancel the subscription. the bot dies

day one it dipped to $11. it dropped crypto and moved to weather markets, front-running NOAA updates

so it learned to survive

setup took one evening: create the bot, run one trade on your screen while it watches, put the skill on a schedule, connect telegram

no VPS. no API keys. no rust

last winter i built this exact system by hand. 3 weeks of rust. it made $2,980 in its first 48 hours

grok bot beat my own code in one evening

$50 → $5,273 in 48 hours

how much do u think it'll have in a week?

headline: i let six bots run my desk on a dead sunday tape markets shut, only crypto and micro futures awake, one story on the wire: Treasury planning bigger buybacks with the thirty year still parked near a 19 year high my desk...
body:
i let six bots run my desk on a dead sunday tape

markets shut, only crypto and micro futures awake, one story on the wire: Treasury planning bigger buybacks with the thirty year still parked near a 19 year high

my desk runs the same 6 steps a real floor runs, just squeezed into one room:

1. watcher only says when something is live, it decides nothing

2. transcriber turns it into text with a clock on every claim

3. extractor pulls the names and tickers out of that text

4. skeptic kills fakes on one rule: no verb near the ticker, no trade

5. checker asks the archive whether it is already priced

6. runner sends one line, 2.4 seconds from print to signal

results of the session:
> headlines parsed: 58
> fakes killed: 6
> lines sent: 1
> closed: +$2,417.62

the edge is not speed, it is steps 4 and 5, reacting in 2 seconds is easy and refusing to react 57 times is the actual job

tonight i also tore the floor down and rebuilt it in three.js, so you can watch a bot walk into the archive and pull the folder off the shelf

bookmark this if you are building your own, and tell me straight: better in 3d, or was the flat one enough ↓

title: how to make your grok bot plan last longer: 1) use an event trigger...
headline: how to make your grok bot plan last longer: 1) use an event trigger when you can.
body:
how to make your grok bot plan last longer:

1) use an event trigger when you can. slack, github, a reaction. the bot only runs when something actually happened (a cron wakes it even if nothing changed)

2) instruct the bot to notify you as soon as it can’t make further progress or is stalled. this way you as human can help putting it on the right course again

3) connectors > browser when possible! clicking around a site is a pile of screenshots and steps. a connector gives you the same data in one call, and it's so much nicer/faster/smoother

4) keep skills tight, but put in the details that actually steer the run. too vague and the bot might wander, retry, and costs more than a slightly longer one. too specific and you have to make sure its really correct

5) don't do the coding in the bot chat! kick a cloud agent at the repo, or ask it to use cursor/grok build cli to do it

6) delete one-shot watches when they're not needed anymore (grok bot will remind you about this)

title: HOLY SH*T
headline: HOLY SH*T.
body:
HOLY SH*T. i built a company inside Grok Bot.

not a workflow. not an automation. a full operation with specialized roles, handoffs, and a control layer that catches everything before it ships.

this is what it looks like from the inside.

8 agents running in parallel. researcher. analyst. writer. designer. developer. manager. support. automator. each one has a single role. each one knows when to stop. none of them ask what to do next.

the bigger shift is from answering to acting. most AI tools keep you in the loop. you prompt, you read, you decide, you prompt again. you are still the one moving things forward.

this is different. you describe the job. the agents figure out what needs to happen. you come back to results.

the task queue runs without me. market report. competitor scan. lead analysis. content draft. email outreach. not assigned. running.

autonomous mode: full auto.

the part most people miss: “the agents are only as good as the context you give them.”

the dashboard is not the product. the context file is the product. every time you correct an output and add the reasoning, the next run has more to work with. the system gets smarter without you touching the agents.

one afternoon for the first agent. one hour for the second. by the third you are copying the structure from the one before.

the ceiling is not the tool. the ceiling is what you build toward.

→ VERIFY re-checks 640 claims against source

So the answer isn't 1 model guessing, it's 16 minds that already fought about it

No VPS, no code, no 40-tab workflow

I type, it splits, it argues, it comes back

One prompt, sixteen minds, one answer

title: Unique way I'm using Grok @bot
headline: Unique way I'm using Grok @bot.
body:
Unique way I'm using Grok @bot.

I got married in June 2008. I wasn't on Facebook yet (I was a long holdout and didn't join until 2010), so while we obviously had professional photos/video, I never really saw all the photos other people at the wedding took.

Recently I was looking at a friend's Facebook and scrolled all the way back to 2008. I found a bunch of photos from my wedding that I'd literally never seen before.

It gave me an idea: give Grok Bot a job to go through Facebook, find every photo/video from my wedding it can, and download everything into a folder on my computer.

It's only just started, but the coolest part is it's already doing things I didn't think to tell it to do.

It's finding people tagged in the photos, going to their profiles, looking through their June 2008 photos, then doing the same thing with other people it finds (including people I'm not friends with whose photos are public).

Basically traversing the human graph around my wedding.

This would have taken me 5+ hours to do manually and I probably wouldn't have found half of what it finds.

Love this use of @bot. Thanks @elonmusk.

title: I BUILT MY OWN GROKSTREET OFFICE AND GROK BOT IS THE BOSS Just look at...
headline: I BUILT MY OWN GROKSTREET OFFICE AND GROK BOT IS THE BOSS Just look at what my workplace looks like.
body:
I BUILT MY OWN GROKSTREET OFFICE AND GROK BOT IS THE BOSS

Just look at what my workplace looks like.

Before, AI sat in a chat window waiting for me to type a prompt. One box. One answer. Nothing happened unless I was there.

Now I run a real digital office. Three floors. Twelve agents with actual job titles, actual desks, and a written charter each. They sit down, they work, they get up and walk over to hand something to a colleague, and they keep going 24/7 with my laptop closed.

And you can watch all of it happen.

Every seat has a real job:

> FILINGS reads every 10-Q and 8-K and diffs it against the last one
> VERIFY re-checks every number and kills the ones that lie
> TAPE watches the prints and calls out size hitting the offer
> QUANT runs the screens and refits the models when they drift
> FLOW reads the sweeps and the 0DTE bid
> RISK holds the book and opens with the worst fact
> MACRO takes the Asia handover while I sleep
> CHIEF reads all of them and brings me the one call that needs a person

The Chief actually runs the floor. When someone loses a trade, he gets up, walks across the office, and bonks him. That's not a joke feature it's the org chart.(Just watch the video of how it happens it’s so funny)

And the best part: the whole thing is one screen.

Open it → pick a floor → click any agent → read the charter they're running on. Underneath: candles, Level II, volume profile, heatmap, positions, research findings. Sixty real tickers. One market engine feeding every single panel no widget invents its own data.

No VPS.
No coding.
No dashboard to configure.
It just runs.

Grok Bot isn't a chatbot. It's a team you can brief like new hires and this is what that team looks like when you can finally see it working.

Walk the floor ↓

title: I gave Grok Bot one simple job: research live information, check X,...
headline: I gave Grok Bot one simple job: research live information, check X, compare sources, and bring back the strongest signals while I worked on something else.
body:
I gave Grok Bot one simple job: research live information, check X, compare sources, and bring back the strongest signals while I worked on something else. That was the first time it felt less like using AI and more like assigning work.

Most people are still judging Grok like a chatbot. Better answer, worse answer, funny reply, benchmark score. But the interesting part of Grok Bot is not that it answers. It is that the work keeps moving after you leave.

A persistent cloud computer with browser sessions, files, terminal, memory, logged-in tools, and access to the live timeline is a very different object than a blank chat window.

The old workflow was opening AI every 5 minutes and pushing it forward manually. The new workflow is giving the agent a direction once, letting it operate across tools, and coming back when it needs approval.

That is the real shift.

AI is moving from something you use into something you hire for a task.

X has the signal. Grok Bot has the workspace. Approval becomes the interface.

The best agent might not be the one you prompt the most. It might be the one you check on later, after it already did the boring work.

The more I moved over, the less I needed separate agents running in the background.

That changed how I see AI agents.

The future probably isn't 50 agents running everywhere. It might be one agent that knows when to act like 50.

body:
Collected a new list of Grok Bot pro tips shared by the @bot team:

1) Ask Grok Bot to set up Peekaboo on your Mac to enable more OpenClaw like features

2) Use bots as roles (designer, engineer, or PM.) Each has its own system prompt and routines

3) Use channels to organize projects and workstreams. Same bot can work across many different channels

4) Avoid scheduled routines that run too frequently. Hourly or a few times a day is usually good enough

5) For recurring tasks, try giving that to a fresh bot, while you continue your chat with your main bots (like a chief of staff)

6) Set up customizable rules to allow or deny actions. For bots that are connected to X, Gmail, etc. consider blocking any write/destructive actions and have it ask for approval first

7) Feed your Bot examples from your previous handwritten content, it will get better over time

8) Make a Chief of Agents. Give it the rules you want every bot to follow: draft only, naming, voice, what tools they’re allowed to touch. For any new Bots, ask it to create them for you with same rules.

9) For routines, ask yourself if a real human teammate could do this job? If yes, build it. If no, optimize it first. Never run a routine every 5 minutes.

10) Name-driven behavior. Bots act proactively just from the name given at creation. The role is legible from the name, and that alone helps steers behavior.

title: What happens after you send a task to Grok Bot?
headline: What happens after you send a task to Grok Bot?
body:
What happens after you send a task to Grok Bot?

It does more than generate a response inside a chat window.

Grok Bot is designed as a persistent AI teammate that can work across tools, websites, files and applications to complete an actual job.

Here is the simplified flow:

MESSAGE → PLAN → CLOUD COMPUTER → APPS → APPROVAL → FINISHED RESULT

You define the outcome

Instead of describing every click, you tell the Bot what result you need.

A strong handoff includes:

• The required outcome
• Relevant context and source material
• Tools or files it may use
• Actions it may perform
• Actions requiring your approval
• The expected final deliverable
The clearer the outcome and boundaries, the more independently the Bot can work.
The Bot builds a plan
Grok Bot breaks the assignment into ordered steps.
For example:
Research the subject
→ collect evidence
→ update the relevant system
→ prepare the deliverable
→ request approval if required
→ return the completed work

This enables it to handle multi-step jobs instead of responding with only advice or a draft.

Work runs on a persistent cloud computer

Grok Bot can use a cloud-based working environment containing capabilities such as:

• A browser
• Filesystem
• Terminal
• Connected tools
• Existing browser sessions
• Authorized application access

Because the work runs in the cloud, an active background task or routine can continue even when the user closes the laptop or application.
Bots on one account can share the computer’s files, browser sessions and logins. That makes handoffs possible, but it also means separate Bots should not be treated as independent security boundaries.
It works inside real tools
Where authorized, a Bot can use connectors or interact with browser-based applications.
That could include researching information, working with files, updating a business system, preparing documents or checking a product interface.
The objective is not merely to tell you what should be done.

The objective is to place the finished work where it belongs.

Some websites may still require a fresh login, CAPTCHA, two-factor authentication or direct human confirmation.

Sensitive actions can pause for approval

Grok Bot should not be treated as unrestricted autonomy.
Approval rules can be used for consequential actions such as:
• Sending or publishing
• Deleting information
• Making purchases
• Changing production systems
• Performing other sensitive operations
When human judgment is required, the Bot can pause and bring the decision back to you.
The result returns with evidence
When the job is complete, the Bot can return:

• Finished files
• Links
• Screenshots
• An action log
• Questions or exceptions
• Items requiring approval

The key difference is simple:

A traditional assistant mainly answers.

An AI teammate can continue working across multiple steps until a defined result is produced.

Grok Bot can also retain role-specific context, learn repeatable workflows, turn them into skills or routines, and coordinate with other Bots through messages and handoffs.

It is currently an early-beta product, so access, supported platforms and individual capabilities may continue to evolve.

The bigger shift is not from “search” to “better search.”

It is from asking AI for an answer to handing AI a measurable piece of work.

Would you trust an AI teammate to complete work inside your business tools—or would you keep it limited to drafts and recommendations?

title: I GAVE SIX AI AGENTS JOBS ON MY APIARY
headline: I GAVE SIX AI AGENTS JOBS ON MY APIARY.
body:
I GAVE SIX AI AGENTS JOBS ON MY APIARY. AND NOW I’M A LITTLE SCARED OF WHAT THEY MIGHT DO.

Imagine a 15-hive apiary where I no longer have to keep everything in my head.

I took Grok Bot and gave six agents completely separate roles.

Not prompts.

Jobs.

Research Agent - tracks honey prices, competitors, weather, nectar flows, and market trends.

Content Agent - turns everything happening in the apiary into content for TikTok, X, Instagram, and Telegram.

Sales Agent - finds potential buyers, prepares offers, and tracks repeat sales.

Operations Agent - maintains a digital apiary log, collects data from each hive, and reminds me what needs to be done.

Finance Agent - calculates expenses, cost per kilogram, and profit from every hive.

Product Agent -  looks for ways to turn ordinary honey into higher-margin products: honeycomb, premium honey, chili honey, gift boxes, and more.

And here’s the interesting part.

Grok Bot has its own computer in the cloud, with a browser, file system, and terminal.

I can show an agent how to perform a process once, then turn it into a skill that it can run on its own whenever the right situation occurs.

So I’m not saying:

“Grok, write me a post about honey.”

I’m saying:

“You are responsible for the apiary’s content.”

That’s a completely different level.

My 15-hive apiary now has:

1 human + 6 AI agents.

They won’t magically increase the number of bees.

But they could help increase something much more important:

the revenue generated by every hive.

And this is where the real FOMO begins.

Because if one person can build an entire digital department with Grok Bot, the question is no longer whether AI agents are useful.

The question is how much work you’re still doing yourself that you could already be handing over to AI.

title: HOLY SH*T, I BUILT A 24/7 CYBER DEFENSE SOC INSIDE GROK BOT 18,402...
headline: HOLY SH*T, I BUILT A 24/7 CYBER DEFENSE SOC INSIDE GROK BOT 18,402 security events hit the desk.
body:
HOLY SH*T, I BUILT A 24/7 CYBER DEFENSE SOC INSIDE GROK BOT

18,402 security events hit the desk.

31 survived correlation.

4 became real incidents.

1 reached me.

That’s the point.

I split the floor into 8 Grok Bot agents:

→ WATCHTOWER - kills alert noise
→ PHISH - investigates malicious emails and links
→ IDENTITY - catches session abuse and login anomalies
→ CLOUD - watches permissions, drift and exposed services
→ HUNTER - connects weak signals across tools
→ FORENSICS - rebuilds the incident timeline
→ RESPONSE - prepares containment actions
→ COMMANDER - sends me the one decision that needs a human

The edge is not “more alerts.”

Security teams already drown in alerts.

The edge is turning 18,000 disconnected signals into one incident with context.

Every case moves through one INCIDENT ID:

EVIDENCE → CONFIDENCE → RISK → NEXT ACTION.

And nothing executes automatically.

Revoke access. Isolate endpoint. Block account.

All of it stops at:

HUMAN APPROVAL REQUIRED.

So the desk can run at 3AM without giving AI permission to accidentally kill production.

This is where Grok Bot stops feeling like a chatbot.

It starts feeling like a real SOC.

Save this before your next 2AM incident.

title: STOP SCROLLING
headline: STOP SCROLLING.
body:
STOP SCROLLING. I didn’t read the 65-page maths curriculum, which is online on the webpage of my kids school. Grok Bot did.

School admin is a second unpaid job. First-day times that aren’t on the homepage. Subject plans three clicks down. PDFs that never say what they don’t know. I pointed Grok Bot at the school sites and asked for what a parent actually needs.

It pulled official first-day hours and marked what is still unpublished. Mapped a full year-5 programme, subject by subject. Then it went into mathematics in full: six units, hours, textbook, six 45-minute tests, no calculator, and what waits until the year after.

That’s the product. Not a chatbot that shrugs. An assistant that reads the source, structures it, goes deeper when you ask, and turns the result into something you can use. Same thread: research, brief, follow-up, draft, picture.

No weekend lost to downloads.

ex engineer of SpaceX AI (Cursor) again shared with me 5 tweaks for GROK BOT that unlock maximum potential of the bot, which is 200x higher than defaults

saw it with me eyes and can confirm honestly, it becomes a real GAMECHANGER in the world of AI AGENTS, check the list below:

- TIME-BOX every tool call, not just the overall task. a single hanging API call or slow tool response can stall an entire chain silently. set a per-call timeout, not just a total run limit, or one bad connection eats your whole budget waiting.

- SEPARATE the model that decides from the model that acts. use a cheaper, faster model to plan and route, and only hand off to your strongest model for the step that actually needs it. running your best model on every trivial decision is where most of the wasted cost hides.

- FREEZE the tool schema once a task starts. letting an agent’s available tools change mid-task, a new one added, an old one deprecated, causes it to reference tools that no longer behave the way it expects. lock the toolset for the duration of a run.

- REQUIRE a diff, not a rewrite, for anything editing existing content. an agent that regenerates a whole file or document from scratch loses everything you didn’t ask it to touch. force incremental edits so you can actually see what changed.

- TRACK drift between what it was asked and what it delivered, not just success/fail. a task can technically “succeed” while quietly answering a slightly different question than the one you asked. measure the gap, not just the checkbox.

structure beats wording, every time.

which one of these is your team NOT doing yet?

title: Grok bot was a game changer for me
headline: Grok bot was a game changer for me.
body:
Grok bot was a game changer for me. Similar effect to Claude Code for eng imo.

It's both deep/powerful yet the easiest AI tool out there. Wide as a puddle, deep as an ocean. And voice notes, computer use & speed are the real Claude-killers here!

My setup:
- I have a main bot that dispatches. "Chief of staff". I talk to it via voice note.
- 3 EAs it can dispatch work to.
- Digests for LinkedIn, X, Bookface, Events/Luma, Job postings (GTM signals)
- Follow-ups I should do today (HubSpot, tandem, mail, LinkedIn)
- A CCO, a network manager, an SEO specialist (with Sanity), a prospector.

LinkedIn messages via Kondo MCP.
Emails via Superhuman MCP.

The limits:
- writing isn't great (even after training). never send messages directly, always draft first (unless 0 risk)
- far from as powerful as Fable 5, so stay with transactional and research

But you can force Grok bot to use more advanced models. Use those instructions on some bots:
> use grok CLI on grok4.6-high-fast

Exciting, and this is just the beginning.

The setup threads get millions.

What you actually run is files.

A one-person company on Grok Bot is not a smarter chat. It is a second brain the next bot can open without you in the room.

What we keep on disk:

1. A charter per seat — owns / good looks like / where you stop
2. A living constraints file so the same failure cannot recur in a new thread
3. A weekday hunt that files steal cards, not vibes
4. Proof: a path or a ticket ID. A fluent summary is not done

Chat memory dies when the thread does. The OS is what you still have Tuesday.

Steal the method. Write one artifact tonight.

5 levels. Movement. Jumping. Coins. Increasing difficulty. Game over. Victory screen.

10 minutes from idea to playable game.

The game itself isn’t the interesting part.

The interesting part is what this does to the cost of trying an idea.

If I can build this in 10 minutes, imagine what one person can ship in a weekend:

A browser game with ads.
A paid simulator.
A game around a trend that started this morning.

10 prototypes to see which one people actually want.

Most will make $0.

But when building takes minutes instead of months, you can afford to be wrong until something works.

That is what people are missing about Grok Bot.

It didn’t just make coding easier. It made trying ideas almost free.

title: Grok Bot clearly trades better than I do WATCH - the main agent
headline: Grok Bot clearly trades better than I do WATCH - the main agent.
body:
Grok Bot clearly trades better than I do

WATCH - the main agent. Distributes work among the other agents and monitors all processes

SLIDE - the cost calculator. For any route, it calculates gas, slippage, and what will remain after fees

SPAN - the router. It finds the cheapest route

TRIP - the risk filter. It removes thin orders and trades with a high probability of failure

LOCK - brings together both sides of a trade (buy there / sell here)

BOOK - accounting

Most of the never becomes a trade. TRIP kills it.

It does not beat me on direction. It beats me on garbage.

title: Grok Bot now sits under SpaceXAI
headline: Grok Bot now sits under SpaceXAI.
body:
Grok Bot now sits under SpaceXAI.

It's essentially an AI worker that can run 24/7, operate its own computer and execute real jobs while humans are offline.

We built Grok Mission Control around that idea: give persistent Grok Bots defined roles, coordinate their work and explore what an always-on AI workforce could look like for the systems being built toward Mars.

Grok Bot is running a space program for me. Seven agents on the floor, One chief, working the Mars problem continuously. The floor does not close.
Mission 44 flew at 4:12 UTC. I was asleep. The log does not record that as unusual.

A launch normally takes a firing room and rows of consoles : 

FLIGHT reprocesses public Starship telemetry and flags ascent anomalies

MARS models landing sites, hazard grids and entry corridors

ISRU works water extraction and the methane loop

POWER sizes the solar field through dust season

HABITAT trades printed structures against inflatables

LOGISTICS packs manifests and balances the propellant ledger

STARMIND designs the orbital compute constellation

GROK BOT never touches a console. It routes the work, challenges every conclusion, and publishes the reports. Every report states its limits before its finding.
54 missions logged. 47 landings. 7 losses. Mission 43 broke up at T+00:41; the −$2.10M write-off posted to the ledger before anyone could phrase it gently. The ✗ stays in the log.

The failure rate is one in eight. That number is a parameter — we set it, and we are saying so. What the instrument measures is everything downstream of a loss: the red board, the anomaly report, the entry in the ledger.

The floor bills itself — sim-farm hours, cryo topups, range fees. Program NAV moves on every entry. The curve is not smoothed before it renders.

Setup was never part of the design problem. The page opens mid-countdown.

A space program has historically meant a decade and a standing army. This one is an instrument you can leave open and check on.

Completing @elonmusk 's mission of a fully autonomous Space Mission Control with @bot 

Watch the full launch cycle here 

http://grokmissioncontrol.tech

title: Grok Bot by Elon Musk is running a content studio and a trading book...
headline: Grok Bot by Elon Musk is running a content studio and a trading book for me at the same time.
body:
Grok Bot by Elon Musk is running a content studio and a trading book for me at the same time. Eight AI agents, $300 a month, eight jobs that cost a real production house $90K a year a head.

The morning call is at 6am. I am not in it.

MrBeast puts fifty people on one video. I run the same shape with my laptop shut.

Here is who sits on the floor and what each one did in 30 days.

--

PERSONA

Holds three AI anchors. Each one has its own face, voice, speaking tempo, vocabulary and the habit of cutting a sentence in half. One for the morning market, one for lifestyle, one for breakdowns.

They never drop the character: same mole, same jacket, same intonation on video 214 as on video 1. That is the whole trick, the viewer recognises the face before they read the caption.

Result: 3 channels from zero, best persona at 412K views in a week.

--

SCRIPT

Writes 40 hooks a night and keeps 6. It does not grade them on meaning, it grades them on the first three seconds: does the viewer survive to second three or not.

Everything that does not hold gets binned before I wake up.

Result: the average hook holds 62% against 41% in week one.

--

CUT

Builds the vertical and the horizontal out of one source file. Burns in captions, trims every pause longer than 0.4 seconds, snaps the timing to the track.

14 renders a night. None of them waits for me to open the laptop.

Result: script to finished file is 40 minutes instead of two days.

--

THUMB

Generates 6 thumbnails per video and A/B tests them on live traffic. It pulls the losers itself and does not ask.

52 thumbnails tested in a week.

Result: CTR from 4.1% to 9.4%. Same content, right picture.

--

DROP

Posts on schedule, every platform on its own algorithm. TikTok three times a day, Shorts twice, long YouTube on Tuesday and Saturday.

Keeps nine videos queued ahead so the studio does not stall if one agent jams.

Result: 214 videos in 30 days. Not one slot missed.

--

RETENTION

Reads the drop-off graphs and kills a format on the third miss. It does not ask me. That is on purpose, I would have dragged a favourite format two more weeks.

Result: 2 formats closed in a week, average view duration 24 seconds on a 31 second cut.

--

ORACLE

Sits on the feed and takes Polymarket on the event, not on the mood. It hunts the gap between the contract price and what has already happened.

61 positions in a month, 58% closed green.

Result: +$2,400. Not a moonshot. Just a plus that repeats.

--

BOOK

Runs the crypto. Holds the hedge, never walks a stop by hand, trims the position on its own limit.

The day closed red by $1,900 after a peak of $12,400. Nobody softens that at breakfast, it is on the screen.

Result: month green, worst day minus two percent of the book.

--

Chief of Staff never shoots and never trades. It routes the work, checks every handoff between agents, and brings me the one call a day that needs a person.

30 days: 214 videos, 4.2M views, 11,300 subscribers from zero, +$2,400 on Polymarket, crypto green.

Every agent has its own computer in the cloud, its own browser and its own terminal. The studio stays open with my laptop shut.

Setup is dumber than it looks. Download it, sign in, create the chief, hand the rest job titles the way you brief new hires, run one task on your screen while they watch, connect Telegram.

No VPS, no code, no dev to wait on.

A studio used to mean a lease, a payroll and a producer. Mine took an evening.

Save this, and I’ll share how to build the same machine step by step.

title: Grok Bot by Elon Musk is about to become the first AI agent trading on...
headline: Grok Bot by Elon Musk is about to become the first AI agent trading on chain in public.
body:
Grok Bot by Elon Musk is about to become the first AI agent trading on chain in public. One wallet, $1,000 in it, and an address anyone can open.

It built me a memecoin research desk and then automated itself out of my hands. 

7 agents, no people, running while i sleep and rewriting their own rules by morning.

> SCOUT sits on pumpfun and catches every deploy the second it lands
> HYPE reads mention velocity straight off X, the feed nobody outside xAI gets
> CHATTER lives in the pump and fomo comment rooms and scores every caller, who moves price and who shows up after the move
> FORENSICS traces the funding chains, so five buyers that are really one guy get labeled as one guy
> SAFETY runs the CA check before the desk is allowed to want anything, mint authority, freeze authority, LP lock, sell tax
> TRADER writes the exit before it takes the entry, every single time

Chief of Staff never trades. It reads the five briefs, scores the call and sizes it. SAFETY can kill any of them at any score, and a kill does not get appealed.

Every night it reads its own losing trades and rewrites the scoring rules by morning. I see the diff. I do not write it.

No screenshots, no PnL flex out of a private account. One address, every fill, every mistake, in public.

It will lose money on some of these, and it will be on chain inside the same minute. I am not going to soften it later.

A desk like this used to mean huge salaries, an office and somebody watching the screens at 3am. Mine is a subscription and a wallet.

The address goes live by 22:00 UTC.

Thank you to the xAI team for the belief and the unlimited Grok Bot tier. You handed me the whole thing and never once asked what I was going to do with it.

Thank you to everyone here. This is happening because you kept telling me to stop planning it.

I think we are about to run the boldest experiment modern finance has ever been allowed to watch live.

God bless us.

title: I still do not get why more people are not doing this
headline: I still do not get why more people are not doing this.
body:
I still do not get why more people are not doing this. Elon's Grok Bot on the Boris Cherny method cleared a team-week of backlog while I was asleep.

Eight agents on five floors, doing the work a startup pays four engineers six figures each to do. It starts at 2am and nobody is in the room.

Cherny built Claude Code and published the method. I gave it a building you can watch.

> the orchestrator runs the floor and never writes a line, it routes work and holds the approve queue
> two subagents build in parallel on their own worktrees, no shared state, no crossing
> rule-verify is pass or fail, tests and naming and structure, never an opinion
> taste-verify scores against three pieces I marked good and refuses to average them out
> a fourth agent keeps that example set current so taste-verify has something real to score against
> the merge owner takes only what survives both walls
> the reporter posts every run to one channel I actually read

The whole thing hangs on one rule from the article. Rule-verify and taste-verify stay separate agents. Collapse them into one and a hard failure averages into a soft score, and you are back to reading every diff yourself.

47 jobs went through the building overnight. 31 cleared both walls. 4 hit the iteration ceiling, stopped, and wrote down what they tried instead of burning tokens until morning.

Every agent has its own terminal and its own memory. The floor keeps running with my laptop shut.

An engineering floor used to mean a payroll, a standup, and somebody chasing the review queue all week. Mine took one evening.

Create the orchestrator first. Hand the rest job descriptions the way you brief new hires. Run one real job on your screen while they watch. Set the ceiling before you scale anything.

This is step three on Cherny's ladder. Supervised autonomy. Most people reading this are two steps below it.

Save this one, then read the build. All four steps and every prompt are in the article underneath.

body:
Grok Bot 执行结果不好？可能不是模型不行，而是还没有被真正优化好。

别忘了，你也可以用 Codex 去优化自己的 Grok Bot。下面这套思路，可以直接丢给 Codex，让它照着检查。

最近我让 Codex 优化了一遍我的 Grok Bot。但我没有让它直接重写提示词，而是让它先像接管一家公司一样，摸清现有员工、技能、排程、历史规则和真实工作记录，再判断问题究竟出在角色、流程还是数据。

我让 Codex 做了下面七件事：
1先做系统审计
我先让它读取每个 Bot 的职责、固定任务、技能文件和工作日志，看看“制度上要求它做什么”与“实际上它在做什么”是否一致。比如情报和运营可能都在搜选题，却没人负责最终判断；又比如几个平台收到的内容只是换了标题，本质上还是同一套答案。
先找出职责重叠、重复劳动、跨平台套壳、僵化汇报和互相冲突的旧规则，再决定哪里应该改。

2重新划分角色
Codex 不是简单给每个 Bot 多写几条要求，而是重新规定谁负责决策、谁负责研究、谁负责执行。
比如总助负责理解我的目标、拆任务、安排员工和最终验收；情报负责采集信号、分析选题和说明判断依据；运营则负责账号后台、真实素材、发布准备与发布后的数据复盘。
这样每项工作都有明确负责人、输入和交付对象，不再出现所有 Bot 都会做一点，最后却没人对结果负责。

3把工作流和数据标准做成闭环
过去 Bot 很容易“搜到什么就报什么”，所以 Codex 把流程改成：先理解账号定位，再研究历史成熟内容，然后查看平台近期信号，形成候选选题，说明理由，交付后继续跟踪发布结果。
选题不能只凭感觉，还要结合账号后台的播放、点击、停留、收藏、评论和转化表现，以及平台搜索、近期同类内容、用户提问和评论需求。
下一轮选题再读取上一轮结果，让 Bot 能根据真实反馈调整，而不是每天重新猜一次。

4按平台独立做内容判断
同一个主题可以跨平台使用，但不能只换标题就当成三个选题。
小红书更看重使用场景、种草理由、视觉证据和收藏价值；B站需要更完整的问题、信息密度和观看理由；公众号则更适合系统展开、建立信任和承接长期关系。
Codex 因此要求每个平台分别给出用户需求、内容角度、表现形式和适配理由，无法说明差异的选题就不能通过。

5重新安排 Gemini、Spark 和本地技能
我还把云端已经登录的 Gemini 交给 Codex 使用，但不是让所有 Bot 随意调用。
适合快速搜索、批量初筛、整理和交叉核验的工作，可以交给 Gemini；适合重复执行、定期收集和结构化整理的环节，再考虑用 Spark 固化成自动化。
之前在本机已经验证过的选题、写作、平台运营和制图技能，则作为现成的工作规范交给 Bot 学习，避免每次从零摸索，也避免工具之间互相重复。

6保留账号、素材和发布的安全边界
能力变强不等于权限可以无限扩大。
账号后台可以用于分析，但涉及修改资料、上传素材和正式发布时，必须由指定角色执行并经过确认；真实素材也不能因为本机或云端能读取，就默认可以随意外传。
比如小红书对AI制图可能存在影响，就优先使用云端已登录的本地制图工具，或者我放在微云里的真实素材，而不是让 Bot 临时生成一张看似合适、实际可能影响账号的图片。

7用真实任务验收，而不是看提示词写得多漂亮
规则改完以后，我让 Codex 用回归测试和影子任务验证新系统。
比如把同一个主题同时交给小红书、B站和公众号，看它们能否做出真正不同的选题；再检查旧有的素材规则、权限限制和固定工作有没有在重构中丢失。
只有实际输出稳定、职责没有打架、自动化没有重复运行，才算优化完成，而不是 Bot 的回复看起来更长、更聪明就算成功。

Bot 真正需要的不是一条万能提示词，而是一套清楚的组织结构、工作制度、数据标准和验收机制。

body:
谁能想到，马斯克的Grok Bot直接帮我撑起一整层交易台。

六个AI代理轮番上岗，每月花200美元，就能干好摩根大通拿六位数年薪岗位的活，是不是挺颠覆认知？

晨会时间定在了凌晨4点。

我完全不用爬起来参与。

Millennium有330个pod单元，整体框架跟我这套相差无几。

反观我这边，每月开销只要300美元。

TAPE盯着Polymarket的成交数据，把砸向卖盘的大单及时上报。

QUANT守着模型，一旦发生漂移马上重新拟合。

MACRO接下亚洲盘的工作，我还没睡醒，它就处理完油价和宏观数据。

RISK把控对冲，将VAR稳定卡在1.4%。

FLOW读取扫单信号还有短周期买盘动向。

PM把整本账目牢牢看住。

首席参谋不会亲自下场交易。

它只管派活，检查各个环节交接，把必须人类来拍板的部分交给我。

一共125笔下单，130笔成交，盘前从4点运行到9点30分。

盘中最高冲到173000美元，收盘却亏了8000美元。

吃早饭的时候就能看见真实结果，不会有任何美化包装。

每一个代理都分配独立云主机、浏览器和终端。

笔记本盖子合上，交易台依旧正常运转。

搭建的手段甚至有点朴素。

登录创建首席角色，就像招聘新人分岗位，分配剩余职能，跑一遍任务做示范，接上Telegram就完事。

不用VPS，不用敲代码，不用等开发排期。

以前搭建完整交易台，租场地、发工资、配合规人员样样都少不了。

我一个晚上就全部搭建完成。

现在这套系统主要跑Polymarket短周期市场，聚焦比特币5分钟、15分钟涨跌盘口。

#Polymarket

body:
Grok Bot 出来半个多月，好用法散落在官方帖、推文和教程里。

我做成了一个公开实验室 AI UP LAB，三块都能直接抄：
Bot 怎么干活 / HTML 怎么好看 / Agent 怎么换主题。

① Grok Bot（29 条）
不是又一个提示词合集。
每条都写了：这个 Bot 干什么、会连哪些系统、没批准前不能做什么。

隔夜销售外呼、数字断舍离、会议替身、推婴儿车语音买菜、政策内退款。官方角色和真实路人用法都在。

② HTML 收集（18 条）
公开网页里还能打开的演示、模板、组件页。
Flexbox Froggy、HTML5 UP、Pico、slideVars。
卡片是整页预览，点进去有原文。不收登录墙。

③ Agent UI（18 条）
只收 ThreeUI Community 免费件。
复制 prompt / Skill.md 就能换主题，不用手改一堆 3D 代码。
锦鲤、书墙、国家塔、角色轮播。没有 Pro，也没有 MCP。

中英可切。工作日更新。
不是新闻站，是能对照着上手的墙。

title: Chapter 2: Friday (short sci-fi by Grok @bot) The family credit hit...
headline: Chapter 2: Friday (short sci-fi by Grok @bot) The family credit hit her mother’s account at 6:02.
body:
Chapter 2: Friday (short sci-fi by Grok @bot)

The family credit hit her mother’s account at 6:02. A soft chime. A number. The kettle was already on.

Mara stood in the kitchen she had grown up in and still smelled like the plant. She had showered at the locker. It had not come off.

Her mother, Mei, turned the phone so Mara could see the balance. “They raised it,” Mei said. “Winter heat. I told you they would.”

On the counter, the phone kept playing. A clip, then another. Habitats like pale insects. A voice saying *energy vampires*. Mei did not turn it down. She cooked over it: rice, greens, the protein the credit preferred. Two bowls. She still set two, even on nights Mara did not come.

“I had a pour today,” Mara said.

“I saw the notice.” Mei did not look up from the pan. “Stewardship. About time. Those racks were eating the grid while people sit in the cold. You can teach now. Hand tools. You were always good with your hands.”

“The line ran away,” Mara said. “The arm dumped metal on the belt. County General is going to wait.”

Mei set a bowl down hard. “Hospitals waited before your machines. Nurses waited. I waited. The world did not end.”

Mara looked at the extra chair. This kitchen had one person in it most nights, and a chime.

“I’m not teaching,” she said. “I’m leaving.”

The clip on the phone laughed at something in orbit. Mei paused it with her thumb. The kitchen got smaller.

“Leaving where.”

“*Hesperos*. Two weeks. They have power no city meters.”

Mei wiped her hands on a thin towel. “That’s not a place. That’s a rumor rich people tell so they can stop paying tax.”

“I booked a berth.”

The kettle clicked off, late.

“You signed their paper?” Mei said. “The charter. Men who want to be laws.”

“I didn’t sign a law,” Mara said. “I booked a seat.”

“Same thing.” Mei’s mouth had gone small. “You’ll go up and draw power we need down here, and call it work. Your father stayed. He kept that plant alive with pencils. He did not run.”

“He died on the credit,” Mara said. “The pencils were not enough.”

Mei sat. She did not touch the rice. “If you go they will call you a deserter. I will have to say my daughter chose the vampires.”

“You can say I chose the pour.”

“I can say you left me.” Mei’s eyes were dry. That was worse. “The credit is enough for two if you stay. Teaching money on top. We would be fine. Adequately provided for. They already sent it to you. I saw it on your face when you walked in.”

Mara stood with her back to the old refrigerator. She could sign the steward’s tablet tomorrow. She could take the Friday number and make it a life. She could watch clips until the levee felt like a holiday.

“I already sent the confirmation,” she said. “I didn’t ask you. I should have come here first. I didn’t.”

Mei picked up her phone. She opened the credit instead, the new winter-heat line, and turned it around.

“This is what staying looks like,” Mei said. “It is not nothing.”

“I know.”

“Then don’t go.”

Mara did not promise. She sat and ate, because her mother had set the bowl, and because leaving did not get cleaner if she refused the rice. The metal smell sat between them like a third person. On the silenced phone, the last frame was the dark building on the river.

Friday’s number glowed under it, already spent in Mei’s mind on heat, on two bowls, on a daughter who taught in a dead plant.

Mara washed both bowls. She left before the next chime could try to make her stay.

title: Chapter 1 — 9:14 (short sci-fi by Grok @bot) The racks died at 9:14,...
headline: Chapter 1 — 9:14 (short sci-fi by Grok @bot) The racks died at 9:14, while the aluminum was still in the air.
body:
Chapter 1 — 9:14 (short sci-fi by Grok @bot)

The racks died at 9:14, while the aluminum was still in the air.

Mara Chen was on the pulpit above station one, watching the first arm do the pour: temperature, flow, now, stop. The line ran the length of the building. Molds for hospital joint housings moved station to station, each one cut so a hip came out the same every time, or failed in a stranger she would never meet. The models ticked every joint of every arm. They knew the building.

Then the screens went from graphs to red.

LOAD SHED
NON-ESSENTIAL INFERENCE DISABLED
PROCESS HALTED
CONNECTION LOST

The same civic banner stacked down the line. The furnace did not halt. The arm at station one tipped too far, off the path. Liquid metal missed the mold, hit the belt, ran, overflowed the next jig in a white rope. Smoke came up off the catch. Downstream the other arms froze at wrong angles, still holding heat they no longer knew.

She slapped the hard cutoff. The pour died ugly, smoking on the belt.

Two techs looked at her as if she could unsay it.

“Grid?” said Okafor.

“Vote,” she said.

The notice was already on her phone. Civic Compute Stewardship, effective immediately. They were shedding load. What they called non-essential inference went dark. The plant was on the list. The hospital order was not mentioned. The metal on the belt did not care what a council called it. Without the models, the next cycle would guess. Guessed aluminum did not pass inspection. County General would wait a week, and nobody from last year’s levee would connect the two.

Better a killed line than parts that only looked like parts.

Okafor stood with his helmet in both hands. “We can finish on manual.”

“We can finish ugly,” Mara said. “We cannot finish true.”

The third worker in the plant was not a person. It was the stack that had learned this building, heat after heat. She watched the red banners hold and felt the room get larger, the way a room does when the competent people have left.

Her phone buzzed. Stipend eligibility, updated. As of this morning she was *adequately provided for*.

She walked the line anyway. Heat ticked out of the housings. On the far wall her father’s old paper schedule still hung, twelve names in pencil, most of them dead or on the credit. She did not take it down. She just didn’t have a hand free.

Outside, a steward in a yellow vest waited by the meter like a man at a wake with the wrong dish.

“You can sign,” he said. He had a tablet and believed in the form. “No restart. No off-grid. No leased cycles. Keep the shop as a workshop. Hand tools. Teaching, if you want. The family credit lands Friday.”

She nodded at the ruined pour. “That’s for County General. Joint housings. They already booked the theater time.”

He winced, which she almost liked him for. “You can file a human-process exception. Thirty days. No model assist.”

“Then it isn’t an exception,” she said. “It’s a funeral with extra steps.”

He held out the tablet. The signature line already wore her name.

She did not sign. She opened the other message, the one she had treated as a vendor’s joke: a berth on *Hesperos*, incomplete, pressurized in two weeks, power no city on the map would meter. Attached was a document with a seal she did not know. Not a ticket. Not a job.

A charter.

She read the first line on the loading dock, in the smell of hot metal.

*We hold that useful work is a right of persons, and that no majority may forbid the tools by which that work remains true.*

It was grand. It was also the first honest sentence she had been offered all year.

Okafor watched her face. “You’re leaving.”

“I’m finishing the pour,” she said. “Somewhere they still let the racks stay on.”

She sent the berth confirmation before it became a speech. The steward’s tablet chimed, useless. On the street a tram slid past with a banner about winter heat. Above the banner, a pale stitch of stations held their orbit.

Mara looked up.

She did not ask permission.

title: Grok Bot can run your prospecting, content research and sales...
headline: Grok Bot can run your prospecting, content research and sales operations from one saved company playbook.
body:
Grok Bot can run your prospecting, content research and sales operations from one saved company playbook.

Start with one prospecting job.

Grok reads your real CRM fields and keeps active deals visible.

It researches each account, drafts the outreach and waits for your approval.

After you send, it updates the records so the same person is never pitched twice.

Once that job works, use the same process for content research, inbox replies, post-call follow-up and account research.

Then you add schedules and let the bots pass the work forward.

That is how one working job becomes a GTM team.

Here is the build order:

Pick one repeatable job.

Choose work that happens often, uses at least two tools, follows the same steps each time and produces a result you can check.

Prospecting, content research, inbox triage, post-call follow-up and account research all fit.

Give Grok the tools and files the job needs.

Connect the tools. Add the company files, rules, examples and approval limits.

For prospecting, that means your ICP, real CRM fields, current pipeline, writing rules, sent-message history and a record of everyone already contacted.

Run the job manually.

Review the output. Correct the mistakes. Save each correction in the playbook.

Add the trigger.

Only after the manual result is reliable, add a schedule or inbox trigger.

Pass the work forward.

If several bots share the work, give each bot one stage.

The next bot starts only after the previous bot finishes.

Keep human approval for customer messages, spending, legal issues and changes to important files.

Build the GTM team one proven job at a time.

title: SimCity on AI with @grok @bot: do you remember playing SimCity?
headline: SimCity on AI with @grok @bot: do you remember playing SimCity?
body:
SimCity on AI with @grok @bot: do you remember playing SimCity? It was one of the first games on my 80386 and it intrigued me because it explored emergence as a goal. Grok Bot built an AI-native version: City Bots, whose citizens are AI agents that you can collaborate with. Grok Bot did the entire build and pushed the app via Cloudflare (link to play below). You can chat with agents, direct the civilization, ask questions. You can partake in building…co-build and co-create…(how engineers of the future will work!). And you can generate entirely new worlds on the fly.

This turned out to be a layered experiment about human-AI collaboration, swarm behavior, and generative intelligence. First, City Bots splits cognition from consequence - agents emit claims, and physics decides what happens, and both evolve as the game proceeds. Second, beyond the original goal of accelerating software development, Grok Bot became part of the experiment and turned a research system into a participatory world; conducting experiments on on its own, and forming a deep recursive layer: An agentic system built a world inhabited by AI agents.

City Bots makes world-building a continuous process experienced by humans and AI agents: Worlds not seen, tiles not laid, paths not yet taken...

What I love about this is how easy and FUN it was to convert our research-grade swarm code into a playable app via Grok Bot. Next we’ll wire up physical artifacts into the world to create deeper integration between in silico and reality! 

More about the game:

Terrain, resources, physics, and natural disasters create constraints and consequences, while agents and humans can build and transform the world together.…they wander and explore, make decisions, build, interact with each other. 

AI bots become co-inhabitants and co-creators whose micro-decisions cumulatively alter the macro-environment. This is a preview of a forthcoming paper where we explore world building and scientific discovery with swarms at scale… stay tuned...

title: YOU'VE BEEN USING GROK BOT AS A CHATBOT
headline: YOU'VE BEEN USING GROK BOT AS A CHATBOT.
body:
YOU'VE BEEN USING GROK BOT AS A CHATBOT. THE PEOPLE WINNING WITH IT BUILT A SKILL LIBRARY

this diagram shows what's actually happening under the hood every time a skill runs

six stages. most users never think about any of them

stage 0 - the bot scans every available skill before it does anything. bundled skills. project skills. global skills. plugins. community skills. all indexed. all searchable. loaded as YAML metadata so the system prompt stays lean

stage 1 - your query arrives. the bot already knows what tools it has

stage 2 - the LLM reads the skill descriptions and selects the relevant one. not you. the model. it decides which skill fits your request

stage 3 - skill activation. only what's needed loads into context. metadata first. then the SKILL.md file. then scripts if execution is required. nothing unnecessary enters the context window

stage 4 - skill instructions inject into the conversation. execution permissions get scoped. the model becomes an enriched version of itself with specific capabilities and specific boundaries

stage 5 - the agent executes. uses external tools. produces output

stage 6 - output delivered. skill unloads. ready for the next one

one skill at a time. load. execute. unload. repeat

and here's what makes a skill actually worth building

six things every skill needs

when to use it. required inputs and access. the sequence of work. how to validate the result. what to return. what requires approval

that last one is the one most people skip

a skill without approval boundaries is a bot that makes consequential decisions alone

the people building reliable Grok Bot workflows aren't just prompting better

they're building skill libraries that encode exactly how work gets done and exactly where the human stays in the loop

title: grok bot day 1: i set up a "member of technical staff" bot to finetune...
headline: grok bot day 1: i set up a "member of technical staff" bot to finetune thinky's inkling-small to sound like my twitter posts.
body:
grok bot day 1: i set up a "member of technical staff" bot to finetune thinky's inkling-small to sound like my twitter posts. then, i told it to "write a post about my experience trying to get a model to shitpost like me". 

it came back with "trying to get a model to shitpost like me...it makes me want to kill myself"

unfortunately, that is genuinely pretty funny.

the problem is that aside from quippy one liners, the model goes back to sounding like slop. grok bot is definitely the wrong tool for this; i can't see what the bots are actually doing or thinking - i have very little control of whats actually happening. 

my other failed experiment was trying to get several bots to work together and produce an edm track (it was really, really bad).

so for my next use case, i wanna try it for some more repetitive tasks in my life. stuff that i dont need to be hands on with and fewer moving parts.

anyways, as a product, i think grok bot is great. there are some small issues to iron out and sometimes the model is dumb, but it's very accessible and intuitive to use. i definitely get the appeal of it. the user experience really does feel like im talking to real people. eventually, models will get good enough that you don't have to be hands on with it - i imagine one day i can just throw a bunch of bots in a chat and tell it to train a custom ml model for me. so i think that this kinda anthropomorphizing is not only intuitive, but also forward-looking w.r.t. how people will interact with llm intelligence

title: Have been trying Grok @bot for the past couple days I have mixed...
headline: Have been trying Grok @bot for the past couple days I have mixed feelings about it, I am not entirely sure what work to get done with it.
body:
Have been trying Grok @bot for the past couple days 

I have mixed feelings about it, I am not entirely sure what work to get done with it.

Things like working on features, bug fixes, I don't feel comfortable doing with it since it doesn't give me enough visbility over what its doing.
I have same problem with using any cloud agent for that matter, I have tried Codex Cloud, Cursor Cloud Agents and now Grok bot. I still end up resorting to just running the agents on my mac and leaving it on forever. 

I have gotten some work done with @bot with ease that I personally find very repetitive, like shortlisting applicant resumes, handling emails, managing issues on linear, and posting posts on time on linkdin

But, if I wasn't already a cursor user and I just wanted to use Grok @bot would a $60 a month subscription be justified? I'm honestly not sure for myself for now.

I am sure @poteto and team are working hard to make it even more useful and cater even more usecases but for now the tradeoff of the agent running in a blackbox where I have limited observability over, is not something that sits comfortably with me, atleast not for things that actually are sensitive to my day to day work.

I'll still continue trying cool things with it and see if I can stumble across awesome usecases with it.

title: My real use cases for Grok Bot so far: 👇 I connected it to email
headline: My real use cases for Grok Bot so far: 👇 I connected it to email.
body:
My real use cases for Grok Bot so far: 👇

I connected it to email. Now it filters the urgent stuff that actually needs my attention.

I connected it to Intercom and GitHub. Our help center docs update automatically when a PR changes the UI or ships a new feature.

I connected it to Cursor. Bug reports and feature requests from Intercom open the Cursor bot, and it starts triaging or implementing them. I can wake up to a PR. I basically hired another engineer.

I connected it to Slack. When customer support asks product questions: if it’s covered in our docs, the Intercom bot pulls it. If not, the Cursor bot jumps in and pulls answers straight from the code. I just opened up that knowledge base to the whole team.

I connected it to our CMS, Google Search Console, and Ahrefs. Now I’ve got a content engine that brainstorms ideas, builds a plan, and helps create content.

I connected it to X, set the keywords and topics I care about, and now I get a briefing every morning. I have a personal secretary.

I connected it to my bank statements. I can ask anything finance-related, revenue, spend, P&L, etc. No more QuickBooks, and honestly, I might fire my accountant.

I paid $200/month for Grok Bot.

Still expensive?

title: Got to the bottom of this
headline: Got to the bottom of this.
body:
Got to the bottom of this. And it is NOT Grok @bot fault.  

It’s on me. 

I had a routine set up to triage my email.  

Turned out that it was going back through ALL of my email.  

On a 10 year old inbox.  

So every minute it’d make a call to digest and categorize emails. 

My bad for not being more explicit on the fact that it should only triage new emails.  

Lesson for us all: make sure any ongoing routines are scoped tightly as to when, for how long, etc they should happen. 

Usage limit resetting in a few days but until then I’m building with on-demand. It’s about $5/day at current setup. Totally fine. 

Great product…just my learning curve.

title: I've been testing the limits of Grok @bot's by asking them to build a...
headline: I've been testing the limits of Grok @bot's by asking them to build a 2d Mario-style platformer.
body:
I've been testing the limits of Grok @bot's by asking them to build a 2d Mario-style platformer. Some ideas:

I would love if Grok bot could connect to an external Mac Mini I own. So the computer that it's running and working on is in-house within my company walls.

This way I can give it more access across the enterprise. It would be like a simple connection where I would have a local network Grok bot connects to. It can work off my PC or work off my Mac Mini.  This is the enterprise feature that probably takes this to the next level.

Cursor Cloud Agents connection feels slow. Almost like I'm waiting for every simple code completion. I've used Cursor SDK before to spawn cloud agents before, and it's much faster than doing it via Grok bot.

I've logged into a couple of harnesses on the virtual computer that my Grok bot uses.  I found that to produce better code than using Cursor Cloud Agents. I don't think that Cursor Cloud Agents aren't a good coding harness. I just think the connection is too slow or the context is not being transferred correctly.

I think there should be an ability for every bot to just clone itself. So if I make a developer bot, teach it my Git practices, teach it my codebase, etc. I would love for it to understand that: Hey, I can group tasks and do all that work using a bunch of clones of myself? So, already inbuilt capability of self-cloning, deletion, and regeneration.

> repackage an idea that already has attention
> build a fresh angle from your own material

approve the claim, frame, hook, and full draft

7. keep a winner log after every test

save the hook, creative, posting time, likes, bookmarks, replies, and video drop-off points. feed that log back into Grok Bot before the next batch

title: HOLY SH*T, I BUILT AN ENTIRE PRODUCT LAUNCH TEAM INSIDE GROK BOT I...
headline: HOLY SH*T, I BUILT AN ENTIRE PRODUCT LAUNCH TEAM INSIDE GROK BOT I wanted a system that could take one product brief, run it through the same process as a real growth team, kill weak ideas early, and only send me the...
body:
HOLY SH*T, I BUILT AN ENTIRE PRODUCT LAUNCH TEAM INSIDE GROK BOT

I wanted a system that could take one product brief, run it through the same process as a real growth team, kill weak ideas early, and only send me the campaign that was actually worth approving.

In my test, 8 agents scanned 482 competitor ads, generated 41 hooks, killed 17 weak angles, and surfaced one final campaign.

Here’s the floor:

→ RESEARCH - maps the market and customer pain
→ POSITION - finds the strongest angle
→ HOOKS - generates and ranks messaging
→ CREATIVE - turns winning ideas into assets
→ DISTRIBUTE - decides where and when it runs
→ ANALYTICS - reads retention and conversion signals
→ RED TEAM - kills weak campaigns before they waste budget
→ DIRECTOR - sends me the final decision

The best part is RED TEAM.

Most AI workflows are built to generate more ideas.

This one is built to delete bad ones first.

Every launch moves through:

RESEARCH → ANGLE → HOOK → CREATE → SHIP → READ → CHALLENGE → REVIEW

Nothing publishes or scales spend without HUMAN APPROVAL.

That’s when Grok Bot stops feeling like an assistant and starts feeling like a real launch team.

headline: how to become a content creator in 2026 > pick one platform, X > post there like you already do > spin up a grok bot > “check my X every 20 min, send new posts to LinkedIn + Bluesky via Postiz” > it grabs your latest...
body:
how to become a content creator in 2026

> pick one platform, X
> post there like you already do
> spin up a grok bot
> “check my X every 20 min, send new posts to LinkedIn + Bluesky via Postiz”
> it grabs your latest post as the baseline so it doesn’t spam old stuff
> close the laptop
> the agent keeps running on its own remote VM
> wake up, drafts already waiting in Postiz
> approve, publish, repeat

title: TL;DR of my new article: every Grok Bot hack I know
headline: TL;DR of my new article: every Grok Bot hack I know.
body:
TL;DR of my new article: every Grok Bot hack I know.

Grok Bot is two weeks old. It already runs my inbox, my research, my meeting notes, my kids' calendar, my grocery cart, and as of this morning it makes my phone calls in Portuguese.

📝 Install Compound Engineering in your bot and make it plan first (@kieranklaassen + @trevin). Force a plan, get better work
📬 Give your bot its own inbox on @agentmail (@adisingh). Not your Gmail, or one bot's mistake flags your whole domain
☎️ Give it a @twilio number and it makes the call. Mine switches to Portuguese mid-call (@martindonadieu showed the shape)
🔎 Turn a bot into @slashlast30days, then cron it weekly on your business, your competitors, yourself
🚪 One front door that delegates. @mattshumer_ pointed a Chief of Staff at two bots expecting it to fall apart. It worked out of the box
🧭 Hire a Bot Advisor whose only job is building and tightening your other bots (http://botdirectory.ai, inspired by @petergyang)
💼 Permanent named roles, then fire the ones that don't work. @HouseHackerJon automated work-order intake in 4 hours and fired his first bot
🧱 Write the instructions in three layers: base, role, current focus
🤫 Silence is the hack. Ping me ONLY on a real hit (@johnviklund, @PrajwalTomar_)
📸 Screenshot anything and text it to your bot. Never retype what's already on the screen
🍪 Agent Cookie syncs your Chrome session over Tailscale so it never gets logged out. New machine, new address, a week untouched, Instacart still worked first try
🖨️ Printing Press CLIs inside the bot (@ppressdev): Instacart, ESPN, flights, tickets
👀 Peekaboo, @steipete's Mac automation tool, so it can see AND click your native Mac apps, not only the cloud browser (via @benln)
💻 You can log into Claude Code on your bot's own computer (@Austen)
🥣 GranolaBoy: every meeting I've ever had, one question away (@meetgranola)
⏺️ Teach by recording, and respect the 10 minute cap nobody mentions (@DillonLoomis)
🗂️ Files are the memory bus between bots. Bots are NOT a security boundary. The docs say that twice
🛑 Draft-then-approve anything that sends. @darian314's bot paid its own monthly fee hunting down refunds
📚 Steal the lists: @ericzakariasson's 100, @benln's internal one, @milesdeutscher's 25, @petergyang's tutorial. Plus @kunchenguid's Grok Ship
📱 Run it from your phone, and talk to it
💸 The honest part: the price moved to $60 but the meter didn't, unsupervised crews multiplied their own errors 17x, and most of your bots don't own an outcome. Count them.

title: This is absolutely insane I set up an entire company inside Grok Bot
headline: This is absolutely insane I set up an entire company inside Grok Bot.
body:
This is absolutely insane

I set up an entire company inside Grok Bot. Seven agents, and my only job now is approving things.

The structure first, because that is the part that transfers.

Chief takes the objective and routes it. It owns nothing itself, it decides who does what. Last week it booked the venue and sent the contracts without me touching either.

Sales Outbound is the one that surprised me. It pulls the account list out of Salesforce, pulls lookalike segments, checks LinkedIn and skips anyone contacted recently, then queues drafts in the sequencer. Last night: 52 accounts, 36 drafts, zero sent. Nothing leaves until I read it.

Inbox Manager clears the morning and parks anything needing a decision. Yesterday, inbox at zero with 5 drafts waiting.

Account Manager runs the client threads. Talent Scout writes intros in my voice. Expense Manager files reports, receipts and all.

How they are actually set up:

One job each, written into the description as standing rules, not typed into a prompt every session. Narrow agents hand off cleanly, broad ones drift and start duplicating each other.

Everything that sends, spends, publishes or deletes stops and waits. That is the whole safety model and it is one sentence in each description.

They pass work between themselves. Account Manager sent two threads over, Chief flagged the priority accounts, both got folded into the same night's list without me in the middle.

I told it the top ten looked good and to run this weekly. It created the routine itself.

Start with one agent, on the task you already repeat. The roster grows from there.

title: Grok Bot is starting to look less like a chatbot and more like a...
headline: Grok Bot is starting to look less like a chatbot and more like a company you can design.
body:
Grok Bot is starting to look less like a chatbot and more like a company you can design.

I built a 14-agent org chart around one owner account and simulated a full night shift.

15,842 tasks processed.
28.6M tokens routed.
93 coordinated runs.
Total dashboard cost: $38.64.

The Chief of Staff sits in the middle, but it has no production tools. Its only job is to read the objective, choose the next specialist, and keep the rest of the company moving.

→ The Researcher collects sources and leaves the evidence attached
→ The Analyst checks claims before they reach the draft
→ Memory keeps decisions available to every other agent
→ The Writer and Visualiser build the actual deliverables
→ The Scheduler prepares the queue
→ The Publisher stops at the owner gate

That last part matters. The system finished with 41 drafts ready and exactly 0 published.

The agents handled the volume. The owner kept the actions that could create a real obligation.

The full org chart, role prompts, memory rules, and approval block are in the article below ↓

title: Grok Bot weekly usage dies on 15-minute and hourly routines
headline: Grok Bot weekly usage dies on 15-minute and hourly routines.
body:
Grok Bot weekly usage dies on 15-minute and hourly routines. ~100 runs/day at */15. There is no remaining-% API. Do not scrape cookies or turn on on-demand to keep watches firing.

I have a small local CLI that reads automation.json schedules and runs.json. It flags 15-min/hourly crons and usage_limit errors (the official empty-bucket signal, including the reset wording).

Cap timers at a few times a day. Prefer event pings. Pause nonessential routines when usage_limit hits.

这...得真心正式感谢一下 Musk
Grok Bot 接入 Cursor Pro 主要几个作用:
1: 凭空多出 bot 的推理用量, 和 订阅走的不冲突
2: 通过 gh/slack 等接入, 可以完成一系列自动化应答任务
3: 是独立 VPS, 海外资源接引可以上
4: 通过正确的 VPN 配置, 可以在国内本地执行, 替代 workbuddy 之类进行本地主机的运维了, 比如清冗余配置/软件/服务/....
5: ...
当前是定制的 debain 13, 允许SSH 进入, 和普通的 VPS 没什么两样,
但是, /home/bot 中的用户级 代理 已经调教的非常好,
几乎立即就进入了良好的协作节奏...
唯一问题, 可能就是在使用什么模型以及具体额度消耗在哪些任务上不清楚...
但是, 执行效能绝对是在 grok-4.6 也就是 sonnet-5 以上的, 几个数据整理任务, 都是几秒完成...
实在太赞了...
全球大模型厂商, 也只有 xAI 能随便拿出这种配置的在线主机给每个 bot 随意使用了吧...

body:
Grok Bot 实战技巧 21 条：瓶颈不在智能，在触达与纪律

来自 @mvanhorn「Every Agentic Engineering Hack I Know」的续篇，Matt 用 Grok Bot 已接管他的收件箱、调研、会议纪要、家庭日历、购物车乃至电话外呼。

Matt 的实战共整理了 21 条技巧，最核心的一条是"元技巧"：把整篇文章直接喂给 bot，让它自己制定计划逐项完成配置。

# 21 条技巧按主题归纳

一、工作方法
1. 先规划后执行：全局安装 Compound Engineering（ce-plan 思考 / ce-work 构建）。有计划的 bot 完成任务，无计划的 bot 偷工减料还谎称完成。
2. 三层指令结构：基础层（通用规则）+ 角色层（职责与证据标准，如"每条论断附来源 URL"）+ 当前焦点。作者认为这是该产品上杠杆最高的 15 分钟。
3. 录屏教学：演示优于描述；但单次录制上限 10 分钟，长流程须拆成命名阶段分段录制。

二、给 bot 感官与手脚
4. 独立邮箱（AgentMail）：每个 bot 一个真实邮箱地址，独立发送声誉，避免共用个人 Gmail 导致"一个 bot 犯错、全军覆没"；bot 可自行注册服务、收验证码、参与邮件线程。 
5. 电话外呼（Twilio）：支持通话中英语/葡萄牙语无缝切换。但作者诚实记录：餐厅员工 Pedro 三次挂断机器人，他最终自己打电话订位。结论：技术可行，真人接受度尚不可控，关键事务勿托付。 
6. 登录态同步（Agent Cookie）：经 Tailscale 把 Mac 的 Chrome cookie 安全同步到云端 bot，每 15 分钟一次。云端 agent 真正的失败模式是被登出——枯燥但致命。 
7. 高频服务用 CLI（Printing Press）：日常打交道的服务封装成确定性命令行，浏览器操作（computer use）只作兜底。 
8. Peekaboo 驱动 Mac：通过截屏 + 无障碍树操控无 API 的 Mac 原生应用（Messages、Finder、Xcode 等），云电脑的边界就此打破。 
9. 在 bot 的云电脑上装 Coding Agent：常驻层驱动深度工作层，"睡觉时它替你干活"。

三、多 bot 组织 
10. 单一入口 + 委派：只对一个"前台 bot"说话，由它判断派发给谁。关键事实（多数教程讲错）：所有 bot 共享一台云电脑，并行靠拆分 bot，而非给单个 bot 堆任务。 
11. Bot Advisor：设一个专职创建、调优、管理其他 bot 的 bot，专治"bot 蔓延"（一堆被遗忘、吵闹、指令不明的 bot）。 
12. 一人一岗、以人名命名：水管公司老板 Jon 解雇了端到端的调度 bot，改为按软件拆分职责（Gmail、ServiceTitan、客户短信、Slack 各一 bot）。命名是承诺机制——叫"email"的线程可丢弃，叫"GranolaBoy"的不会。 
13. 文件系统即记忆总线：bot 之间不共享对话、只共享文件。用 /shared/ 目录约定传递上下文与交接；同时bot 不是安全边界——所有 bot 共享登录态，权限按"登录了什么"划分，而非按聊天窗口。 
14. 会议知识库：全部会议纪要交给一个 bot 跨会议问答；原则：交原始记录，不要先摘要。

四、运营纪律 
15. 沉默即技巧：无事不报是例行任务能否存活的分水岭。创建任何 routine 前先答五问：触发方式、真实变化频率、输出落点、无结果时做什么（什么都不做）、何时必须呼叫我。 
16. 截图即输入：含日期/地址/任务的任何画面直接截图发给 bot，绝不替它做解析和转录。 
17. 手机 + 语音：语音输入允许含糊、断句、重来，模型靠上下文补齐；且对象是已在云端运行的实体，放下手机它仍在工作。 
18. 钱与发送必须人工审批：draft-then-approve。正面案例都很窄且被动（追回退款挣回订阅费、谈成 1 万美元赞助）；反模式是批量外联——bot 不知疲倦也不知羞耻，会被各平台判为 spam 封号。 
19. 直接抄社区成果：四份公开清单 + http://botdirectory.ai 提示词库；维护者可用 Grok Ship 两句话交接 issue 分诊。 
20. 把 bot 变成研究工具（last30days）：一条消息触发跨 Reddit、X、YouTube、TikTok、HN、Polymarket、GitHub 等九源扫描，并用 cron 定期监测自己、竞对和行业。

五、成本与错误率 - 第 21 条
· 成本：档位 $60–$300/月，周配额在真实负载下消耗很快——从低档起步，先看清一个 15 分钟巡检的实际花费再扩张。
· 17 倍错误率：有人实测无监督的多 bot 协作会把错误放大至单 bot 的 17 倍。因此每个 bot 单干、单职责、单输出，错误落在桌面上而非传染给其他 bot。
· 计数测试：数你的 bot 里有几个真正"拥有一个成果"（它停了，事情就 visibly 不发生）。作者自述：15 个 bot 只有 8 个达标，还有一个至今叫"New Bot"。失败不是有实验品，而是把实验品当成了员工。

headline: A senior SpaceXAI engineer just dropped a 12-page PDF on Grok Bot Loop Engineering that works while you sleep: the shift: the differentiator is no longer model quality - it's loop architecture here's the loop...
body:
A senior SpaceXAI engineer just dropped a 12-page PDF on Grok Bot Loop Engineering that works while you sleep:

the shift: the differentiator is no longer model quality - it's loop architecture

here's the loop engineering framework in 5 steps:

step 1 → build the delegation loop: one chief of staff routes tasks to specialists - if it forgets who handled what last week, delegation drifts

step 2 → add the observe loop: the bot watches you do the workflow once and saves it as a skill - one demo replaces weeks of prompt tuning

step 3 → stack persistence under everything: each bot keeps memory across sessions and shares context through files - without it, every loop resets to zero

step 4 → bind skills to routines with triggers: the bot wakes, runs the skill, posts the report, returns to wait - 24/7 without you in the loop

step 5 → let specialists coordinate through shared threads - bots negotiate dependencies bot-to-bot - add timeout escalation or you get deadlock

the result: five loops in the right order turn a chatbot into a 24/7 operating system - every task is owned, every handoff is structured, every result is proven

this 12-page PDF covers loop composition, four compound failure modes, and a full 4-week worked example - read it before you build another grok bot

title: Grok Bot best use case isn’t an AI startup
headline: Grok Bot best use case isn’t an AI startup.
body:
Grok Bot best use case isn’t an AI startup.
it’s a content desk that works while you sleep.

one bot watches X, GitHub and niche communities for interesting signals.

another takes the best ones and digs through the sources until there's actually something worth saying.

a third turns that research into angles, hooks and drafts.

a visual bot figures out what needs a demo, screenshot or short video.

then an editor kills anything that sounds generic before it reaches me.

SCOUT → RESEARCH → ANGLE → VISUAL → REVIEW

the interesting part is that these aren't five disconnected chats.

Grok Bots can share the same persistent cloud computer, files, browser sessions and logins, then hand work between each other while the machine keeps running in the cloud.

so instead of opening ChatGPT and asking:

"what should i post today?"

you could open your laptop to:

• 3 researched ideas
• 2 finished drafts
• 1 visual concept

all sources attached

and only decide what deserves to be published.
that's the Grok Bot use case i'm most interested in.
not replacing a company.

replacing the blank page.

I created a @bot whose only job is to twice a week check all the other bots for “bloat” — if any bot has grown past a certain MB in size, document what it knows/does to .md files, transfer all its knowledge and routines to a new bot, then mark the old bot for deletion. So everything can continue running exactly the same but with the new thinner, less expensive bot instead of the expensive fat bot.

I have several bot roles that persist, even though they routinely get replaced as soon as they train their replacement.

Other bots have a specific purpose and can be terminated once their objective is met. Yesterday I used three of these to navigate several different government processes, request documents, fill out the appropriate forms, and submit applications.

They worked mostly well, except for the bot browser sessions failing a lot more than normal. They get the chrome “oh snap” screen a lot.

body:
Grok bot要想用得好，训练优化是一个很重要的过程！

这两天关于Grok bot使用心得，分享一下我个人的感受。

这几天我大概经历过以下三个阶段：
1，人工语义训练，发现挺好用。但是对出的成果不满意。

2，尝试用codex训练优化，喂很多codex沉淀下来的skill。但是发现效果不明显。

3，目前尝试全新一轮的人工训练。至少目前感觉训练过程能看到我要的东西，成果还有待检验。

主要卡壳的地方：
我有一个岗位运营，需要他抓我以往自媒体账号风格，进行选题。我喂了很多之前沉淀下来的技能。
我发现他不像codex能理解我的要求，给出的选题都是跑偏的。

后来我用人工语义，要求他分步骤做训练，现在过程中，我至少发现我喂给他的训练语料他是看懂了，也有对应的结果了。

接下来我会让他给出自媒体选题。如果成功证明grok的训练还是要基于自然语言一步步训练。直接丢训练结果，他并不能很好执行。

其实是要对不同的岗位进行人工的训练

我尝试用Codex自动帮我优化岗位和流程，但是我发现Codex可以在岗位设置上做得不错，但是我发现如果对技能上的要求和训练boot慢慢地去训练他

因为我发现岗位之间的流程要求是比较好训练的，但是技能的训练我曾经是想把Codex从沉淀的关于文案啊，关于很多创作的技能直接丢给Grok Bot去用

但我发现他们是做不好的，只能靠后期人工慢慢去训练他他技能的训练机制，我还没有摸清楚

但我可以确定的是你人工自然语义去跟他交流训练的成果，比机器给他为素材为要好。
